# CEP Repository and Collaboration Practice

This collaborative report documents Group 1's application of Git, GitHub, Quarto, and Positron during our CEP collaboration practice. Each group member will contribute to the report through the shared GitHub repository using the required pull, edit, render, review, stage, commit, and push workflow.

> **Collaboration principle:** The GitHub repository serves as the group's authoritative version of the CEP project. Each member should pull before beginning work and push completed changes so that the group remains synchronized.

# Prompt 1: Repository Setup and Shared Ownership

**Principal Author:** Mickyas Shawel

Explain how your group created its CEP repository from the MSDM CEP template, selected an appropriate visibility setting, invited collaborators, and ensured that every member cloned the same repository. Clearly distinguish among using a template, creating a repository, and cloning a repository. Why would independently cloning or copying the original template create problems for group collaboration?

Our group established one shared CEP repository by using the MSDM CEP GitHub repository as a **template** rather than cloning the original template directly. Using a template created a new repository specifically for Group 1 while preserving the required CEP file structure and supporting files. We named our repository `CPP-MSDM-CEP-Group-1---CVrx` and selected the appropriate repository visibility based on the confidentiality requirements of the project. The designated repository owner then invited the other group members and faculty lead as collaborators so that everyone could contribute to the same remote repository on GitHub.

It is important to distinguish **using a template, creating a repository, and cloning a repository**. Using the MSDM template provides the starting structure for a new CEP repository, while creating the repository establishes our group's independent remote project on GitHub. Cloning occurs afterward and creates a local copy of that group repository on each member's computer while maintaining its connection to the shared remote repository. If members independently cloned or copied the professor's original template instead, they could end up working from separate repositories or disconnected project copies. Our group instead works from the same repository so that Git can maintain a common history of contributions and allow each member to pull teammates' changes and push their own work back to the authoritative project.

# Prompt 2: Local, Remote, and Working Files

**Principal Author:** Mickyas Shawel

Explain the relationship among the files on your computer, the local Git repository, and the remote repository on GitHub. In your explanation, distinguish among saving, staging, committing, pushing, fetching, and pulling. Why does saving a QMD file on your computer not make the change available to your teammates?

The CEP project exists in several related states during our Git workflow. The **working files** are the files we actively see and edit on our computer in Positron, such as the QMD and rendered HTML files. These files are located inside our **local Git repository**, which allows Git to track changes and maintain a history of commits on our computer. The **remote repository** is the shared version hosted on GitHub. Each group member has their own local clone, but those clones are connected to the same remote repository. This relationship allows us to work locally while using GitHub as the central location for sharing completed changes with the rest of the group.

Several Git actions move changes through this workflow. **Saving** records an edit to the working file on the local computer, but it does not add that change to Git's history. **Staging** selects specific changed files to include in the next commit, while **committing** creates a recorded snapshot of those staged changes in the local repository with a descriptive message. **Pushing** sends local commits to the remote GitHub repository so that teammates can access them. **Fetching** checks the remote repository and retrieves information about new commits without automatically integrating them into the current working files. **Pulling** retrieves remote changes and integrates them into the local branch. Therefore, simply saving our shared QMD file in Positron does not make the change available to teammates. The change must be staged, committed, and pushed to GitHub before another member can retrieve it by pulling the latest version.

# Prompt 3: Document Your Group's Round 1 Workflow

**Principal Author:** Mickyas Shawel

Describe the order in which group members completed Round 1. For every member, report:

- the member's name;
- the section or content added;
- whether the member pulled before editing;
- the commit message used; and
- how the member verified that the push succeeded.

Our group is completing Round 1 sequentially so that each member works from the most recent version of the shared report. Mickyas Shawel began the process by pulling the latest version of the `main` branch and confirming that the local repository was synchronized with `origin/main`. He then created the `Col-Practice` folder and established the initial Quarto report, including the required YAML configuration, essay prompts, collaboration evidence appendix, and the initial responses for Prompts 1–3. After rendering and reviewing the report, the QMD and self-contained HTML files were prepared for the first Round 1 commit.

Table @tbl-round1 documents the Round 1 sequence. The remaining entries will be completed as each group member finishes their contribution so that the final table reflects the actual Git history rather than anticipated activity.

| Order | Member | Section/Content Added | Pulled Before Editing? | Commit Message | Push Verification |
|-----------:|------------|------------|:----------:|------------|------------|
| 1 | Mickyas Shawel | Created shared Quarto report structure and drafted Prompts 1–3 | Yes | `Create collaboration practice report and draft Prompts 1-3` | Verified commit on GitHub after push |
| 2 | Wenting Jiang | Added responses to Prompts 4–5 and restored the Prompt 4 heading | Yes | `Add responses to Prompts 4-5 and restore Prompt 4 heading` | Verified commit on GitHub after push |
| 3 | Tim Arana | Added responses to Prompts 6–7 | Yes | `Add Tim's responses to Prompts 6 and 7` | Verified commit on GitHub after push |

: Group 1 Round 1 collaboration workflow

We chose a **sequential workflow** for this exercise because the group is intentionally practicing collaboration on one shared QMD file. After one member finishes, that member renders, reviews, commits, and pushes the updated report before the next member begins. The next member then pulls the newest version before editing. This reduces the likelihood that two members will modify the same lines from different versions of the document and create unnecessary merge conflicts. It also produces a chronological Git history that makes the authorship and purpose of each contribution easier to identify.

The sequential process can be summarized as:

> **Pull → Edit → Render → Review → Stage → Commit → Push**

Following this sequence gives the next group member a clear handoff point and helps ensure that the shared GitHub repository remains the authoritative version of the report.

# Prompt 4: A Reliable Everyday CEP Workflow

**Principal Author:** Wenting Jiang

Create a numbered checklist that a group member should follow every time they work on the CEP report, beginning before they edit and ending after they push. Explain why pulling before editing and using focused, descriptive commits make collaboration safer and make the project's history more useful.

Our group will use the following workflow each time we work on the CEP report:

1.  Confirm the assigned section and let the group know who is editing.
2.  Open the shared repository and run `git pull origin main` before making changes.
3.  Edit the assigned section and save the QMD file.
4.  Render the report and check that the content and formatting look correct.
5.  Stage the updated QMD and HTML files with `git add`.
6.  Commit the changes with a clear message describing the work completed.
7.  Use `git push origin main` to send the changes to GitHub and make sure the commit is visible.
8.  Tell the next group member that the file is ready.

Pulling before editing is important because another member may have already updated the report. Starting with the newest version helps prevent merge conflicts and keeps us from accidentally overwriting someone else’s work. Clear commit messages are also useful because they show what each person changed. For example, `Add Wenting's responses to Prompts 4 and 5` is more helpful than a vague message such as `update`or `final` provides little useful information. Clear commit messages allow the group and instructor to understand the sequence, content, and authorship of each contribution.

# Prompt 5: Coordinating Work and Preventing Merge Conflicts

**Principal Author:** Wenting Jiang

Explain what may happen when two people edit the same lines of the same QMD file and then attempt to push their work. Describe at least three practices your group will use during the CEP to reduce merge conflicts. Include how your group will divide sections, communicate who is editing, and decide when work is ready for another member.

When two group members edit the same lines of the same QMD file from different local versions, Git may be unable to determine which changes should be retained. The first person may push successfully, while the second person’s push may be rejected because the remote repository contains newer changes. After pulling, the second person may encounter a merge conflict and must compare the current and incoming versions before the file can be committed and pushed safely.

To reduce merge conflicts during the CEP, our group will use the following practices:

1.  We will divide the report into clearly assigned prompts or sections so that each member knows which content they are responsible for.
2.  Only one member will edit the shared QMD file at a time during the collaboration practice. Before beginning, the member will notify the group through Slack or text message that the file is being edited.
3.  Every member will pull the newest version from `origin/main` before making any changes.
4.  Members will avoid editing another person’s assigned section unless the change has been discussed or is part of the required peer-review round.
5.  After editing, each member will save, render, and inspect the complete report before committing and pushing both the QMD and HTML files.
6.  The file will be considered ready for the next member only after the current member confirms that the push succeeded and that the commit is visible on GitHub.

This coordinated handoff process helps the group avoid simultaneous editing and ensures that each person begins with the most recent version of the report. For larger or riskier changes, such as reorganizing several sections or substantially revising the report structure, the group may use a separate branch and pull request so that the changes can be reviewed before they are merged into the `main` branch.

# Prompt 6: Responding to a Push Rejection or Merge Conflict

**Principal Author:** Tim Arana

Consider this situation: A group member edits the report without pulling first. Meanwhile, another member pushes changes to the same section. Git rejects the first member's push, and a merge conflict appears after pulling.

Explain, in order, what the first member should do. Describe how the member would use Positron's Merge Editor or the conflict markers in the file to compare the current and incoming changes, decide what content to retain, remove the conflict markers, render and inspect the report, commit the resolution, and push it. Also explain why force-pushing, deleting a teammate's work, or replacing the repository with an older local copy would be inappropriate.

In a situation when a push is rejected because another team member has already pushed changes, the member should not force the push or overwrite the repository. First, the member should keep their local work and run `git status` to see what the current state of the repository is. Next, they should pull the newest changes from the remote repository. If Git identifies a merge conflict, the member should compare their current changes with the new incoming changes from the teammate. In Positron, this can be done with the Merge Editor. Also, the member can review the conflict markers directly in the QMD file. The member should determine which portions of each version the group wants to keep and combine the correct content when necessary. Finally, the member must remove all conflict markers after resolving the differences.

After resolving the conflict, the member should save the QMD file and render the report again. Rendering is important because a conflict may be resolved from Git’s perspective while still leaving formatting, syntax, or content problems in the report. Next, the member should inspect the rendered HTML, stage the resolved files, and create a descriptive commit explaining the conflict resolution. Then, the member can push the new commit and verify on GitHub that it uploaded successfully. Force-pushing would be inappropriate because it could overwrite changes already made by another group member. Deleting a teammate’s work or replacing the repository with an older local copy could remove contributions and damage the shared project history. The best response is to resolve the conflicting changes so that the repository preserves the work that should remain.

# Prompt 7: Branches, Issues, and Pull Requests

**Principal Author:** Tim Arana

Based on the collaboration video, explain the purposes of a GitHub Issue, a branch, and a pull request. How could these tools support task assignment, review, and approval during a longer CEP project? Contrast this approach with making a small, coordinated change directly on the main branch. Identify at least one situation in which your group should prefer a branch and pull request.

A GitHub Issue, a branch, and a pull request serve different but related purposes. A **GitHub Issue** can be used to document a task, problem, or improvement and assign responsibility for completing it. A **branch** creates a separate line of development where a member can work on a change without changing the main version of the CEP report. When the work on the branch is ready, a **pull request** allows the changes to be reviewed and approved before they are merged into the main branch. Together, these tools provide a structured way to assign work and review contributions before they become part of the primary report.

For a longer CEP project, our group could use Issues to identify and assign larger tasks, branches to complete those tasks without disrupting the report and pull requests to give other members an opportunity to review the work before approval and merging. A small change, such as correcting a typo could be made directly on the main branch if the member pulls first and notifies the group. Our group should use a branch and pull request when making a change that affects multiple sections or requires review before being added into the main report. This approach would allow the group to evaluate changes without putting the main version of the CEP report at risk.

# Prompt 9: Security, Confidentiality, and Repository Hygiene

**Principal Author:** Luis Berumen

Explain what materials must never be pushed to the CEP repository, even when it is private. Address confidential client data, personally identifiable information, passwords, API keys, access tokens, temporary files, and locally generated files that do not belong under version control. Explain the role of `.gitignore`, and discuss what a student should do before proceeding if they are uncertain whether a file may be shared.

There are certain files and information that should never be pushed into our CEP repository even if the repository is private. This includes confidential client information, personally identifiable information, passwords, API keys, access tokens, and any other information that someone should not have access to. Temporary files and locally generated files that are not needed for the project should also not be included in the repository. Having a private repository does give the project more protection but it does not mean that it is safe to upload confidential information into it.

The `.gitignore` file helps with this because it tells Git which files should not be tracked or included in commits. This can help prevent temporary files, credentials, or other files that do not belong in the repository from accidentally being included. However, we should still check what files we are staging before making a commit instead of only relying on the `.gitignore` file. If someone in the group is unsure whether a file or information can be shared, they should not push it and should first ask the group or Professor Moore before proceeding. It is better to check before pushing because once sensitive information is added to the repository it can create security and confidentiality problems.

# Prompt 10: Group Collaboration Agreement

**Principal Author:** *Group 1*

Develop a short Git/GitHub collaboration agreement that your group will follow for the remainder of the CEP.

::: callout-important
## Group 1 Git/GitHub Collaboration Agreement

For the rest of the CEP our group will follow these rules to make sure everyone is working from the same version of the project and to reduce problems when working together:

1.  Every group member will pull the newest version before they begin editing and will push their changes after they are finished, rendered, and reviewed.
2.  We will divide the work between group members so everyone knows what section or task they are responsible for.
3.  Group members should not edit the same section at the same time. We will communicate with each other when someone is working on the shared file and when they are finished.
4.  Commit messages should clearly explain what was changed instead of using messages such as `update`, `changes`, or `final`.
5.  Small changes can be made directly on the `main` branch as long as the group coordinates the work. For larger changes that affect multiple sections or need to be reviewed first, we will use a branch and pull request.
6.  If a push fails or we have a merge conflict, we will pull the newest changes and review the differences before deciding what needs to be kept. We will not force-push or delete another group member's work just to fix the conflict.
7.  Each person should render and check the report after making their changes. Before the final submission, the final editor will pull the newest version, render the entire report, check the links and formatting, and then push the final version.
8.  Confidential client information, personally identifiable information, passwords, API keys, access tokens, and other sensitive information will not be pushed into the repository. If we are unsure whether something can be shared we will check before adding it.

**Group approval:** All Group 1 members have reviewed and approved this agreement and agree to follow it for the remainder of the CEP.
:::
